analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue federal officers for damages when their constitutional rights are violated.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in November 2025 with 37 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a person whose constitutional rights are violated by a federal agent — a border agent, an immigration officer, an FBI agent — generally cannot win money damages in court, because the Supreme Court has narrowed the old Bivens decision that once allowed such suits. This bill would make federal officers suable the same way state and local officers already are under a 150-year-old civil rights law. It has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who are stopped, detained, searched, or harmed by federal agents and want a court remedy, beyond the limited options that exist today after the Supreme Court closed off most federal damages suits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds federal officers to the civil rights statute that already lets people sue state and local officials for money damages when constitutional rights are violated [S2].
It creates a civil remedy for any individual whose rights are violated by a person acting under federal authority, restoring a path to damages that the courts have largely shut [S1][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies and their officers, who would face damages lawsuits and defense costs; if agencies indemnify their employees, taxpayers ultimately share the cost.

drawbacks.text: Individual agents could face personal damages liability for split-second decisions in the field, which supporters of existing immunity argue can deter vigorous policing and border enforcement [S2].

The remedy is a broad statutory change rather than a tailored one, so it would apply across the entire federal workforce acting under federal authority, not just the agencies most often at issue in rights-abuse cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and concrete: a way for people injured by federal agents to win compensation when courts today say none exists. The costs are higher litigation against federal employees and possible caution in enforcement, and the bill does not build in any middle ground between the two. Whether that trade is worth it is a fair policy argument, but with no Republican support it has not received one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has stayed with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: The Bivens Act was introduced on November 18, 2025 by Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia with 14 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action has been taken [S4].
All 37 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and federal officers keep the existing shield from damages suits, since the bill has not advanced.

for.name: Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a damages remedy against federal officers and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 37 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the Democratic side of the chamber.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill since it was referred to the committee.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican has cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat — 37 of 217 House Democrats — and no Republican has signed on, so support splits fully by party.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and immigration agencies
industries.note: The bill would expose agents at agencies like ICE, CBP, and the FBI to damages lawsuits that courts currently block, ending a legal shield these agencies now operate behind. For ordinary people, the shield means there is often no way to be compensated when an agent violates their rights.

industries.industry: Federal officeholders and employees acting under federal authority
industries.note: Any person acting under federal authority could be sued for constitutional violations, a new personal legal exposure for government workers. The public interest in accountability runs against the interest of officials in keeping that protection.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a Republican House majority, and referral to a Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee with no scheduled action, the bill is very likely to remain in committee without a hearing or vote for the rest of this Congress.
